articles.title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain
articles.authors: Kalyan Santra, Kevin Barber, Francesca Logiacco, M. Agustina Frechou, Arash Bellafard, Jyun-you Liou, Alipasha Vaziri
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing
articles.summary: Three-photon microscopy reaches deeper than two-photon imaging, but cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal activity had stopped at about 1.2 mm in the mouse brain. TrUDI extends this to 2.1 mm, reaching the hippocampus and striatum through intact cortex. It delivers fewer but more energetic pulses and fires the laser only on the neurons being recorded, which cuts light exposure by up to 80% and raises efficiency about 250-fold. The authors found no sign of inflammation or DNA damage from the imaging.
articles.why: Population imaging of deep brain structures without removing the cortex above them.

articles.title: Volumetric scattering microscopy
articles.authors: Zijun Gao, Keyi Han, Zhi Ling, Hongmanlin Zhang, Edward A. Botchwey, Wenhao Liu, Xuanwen Hua, Shuyi Nie, Shu Jia
articles.summary: Scattering in tissue scrambles both the position and the direction of fluorescence light, which limits 3D imaging, and existing computational corrections need wavefront sensing or heavy hardware. Volumetric scattering microscopy (VSM) is scan-free: an aperture-segmented Fourier light-field set-up records the volume in one shot and a feature-based descattering step reconstructs it, with no wavefront measurement or mechanical scanning. The authors show reconstructions in phantoms, cells, ex vivo muscle and intact Xenopus embryos with preserved resolution and better optical sectioning.
articles.why: Scan-free 3D fluorescence imaging through scattering tissue with simple hardware.

articles.summary: Serial optical coherence microscopy images a tissue block section by section using its intrinsic scattering contrast. Combined with tissue clearing, it produces whole-organ 3D images with no stains, as a route toward comprehensive 3D histopathology.

articles.title: Video-rate volumetric chemical imaging via mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography
articles.authors: Masato Fukushima, Keiichiro Toda, Yusei Sugawara, Shotaro Kawano, Takuro Ideguchi
articles.summary: Mid-infrared photothermal (MIP) imaging reads molecular vibrations through the slight heating they cause, and optical diffraction tomography (ODT) maps the 3D refractive index of cells. Combining the two, the authors record volumetric chemical images at 19.2 volumes per second, about 400 times faster than before, with a signal-to-noise ratio above 70, and sweep 300 cm⁻¹ of spectrum within one second.
articles.why: Label-free chemical imaging of whole cells at video rate, fast enough to follow dynamics.

articles.summary: Membrane potential (or voltage) imaging in acute brain slices is widely used in fundamental and applied neuroscience even in an age characterised by the surge of in-vivo recording. This optical method remarkably increased its ability in providing key information both at the level of single cell and at the level of populations and networks. But, more importantly, technical progresses occurred in the last two decades enlarged the potential pool of voltage imaging users from relatively few specialists to scientists in many fields including those working in industry.
